name: shotgun-surgery
intent: Records what Shotgun Surgery costs: one requirement has been scattered across a dozen classes, so a single change means a dozen coordinated edits in a dozen files — the price is an unimaginative number of places to forget, each miss a latent defect, and a merge conflict on every shared file.
problem: A logical responsibility has been spread so thin that no class can change for it alone. Adding a menu item means touching the constants file, the delegate-registration table, the UI wiring and the test fixture; adding a field means touching the DTO, the ORM mapping, the view model, the template and the API documentation. Every one of those edits is defensible on its own.
context: Shotgun Surgery is the exact mirror image of Divergent Change, which Fowler and Beck state bluntly: you whiff it when every time you make a change you have to make a lot of little edits to a lot of different classes, and when the changes are all over the place they are hard to find and easy to miss. Refactoring.guru adds the most useful diagnosis — a single responsibility split across a large number of classes, which is exactly what overzealous application of Divergent Change produces, so a codebase can convert one smell into the other in a single refactoring session. Kerievsky named the same structure 'Solution Sprawl'; the difference is only when you notice it (while changing, or while reading the issue). A commonly cited real instance is adding one line number to a log statement across every logging call site in the system.
benefits: One requirement lands in one place: the change becomes a single edit, and 'did I get them all?' stops being a question you have to answer by memory.
Misses stop being silent defects. Every forgotten call site in the scattered version is a bug that survives review because nothing in the diff shows what was missed.
Merge conflicts collapse. A change confined to one file conflicts with one file, not with every team touching the subsystem.
The knowledge becomes reusable. Once the duplicated knowledge is one function, the next caller gets it for free instead of re-implementing it.
The fix cost of a defect drops: a bug replicated in twenty call sites is twenty bug reports and twenty patches.
tradeoffs: Cohesion is the thing being restored, and cohesion means larger units. Fowler and Beck are explicit that a useful tactic is to inline first — Inline Function or Inline Class — and accept a temporary Long Method or Large Class, because a big coherent unit is easier to reorganise than fifteen thin scattered ones.

Gathering scattered behaviour can create a god object, which is the documented way this refactoring goes wrong. Refactoring.guru's own sequence is Move Method/Move Field into a single class, and Inline Class if the originals are left empty.

The extraction is often a real design decision, not a mechanical move. Knowing *which* class should own a cluster of functions is judgement work, and the wrong choice bakes an incorrect boundary into the code.

Some scattering is irreducible. Cross-cutting concerns (logging, auth, metrics) genuinely apply to every call site; duplicating them in every call is worse, which is why the industry answer is Aspect/decorator/interceptor-shaped rather than 'move it somewhere'.

Collecting scattered state behind a richer interface can enlarge every signature. Fowler's remedy for functions transforming a data structure is Combine Functions into Transform, which produces one stage of a pipeline rather than one god class.
Sometimes the right answer is not to consolidate but to delete. A requirement spread across nine files often means nine features that were never really one.
quality_attributes_note: Scores describe the codebase while the smell is present. Performance and scalability stay high because scattering changes is not a runtime property — the smell costs you at the moment of change. Extensibility is the lowest axis because the structure's central promise is that one requirement cannot be added in one place. Observability is mid: scattering frequently means the same log line, metric or trace attribute is emitted from many call sites with subtly different values, which is what makes production triage slow.

participants.responsibility: One requirement — a menu item, a log field, a new attribute, a validation rule — whose implementation is split across several classes.
participants.notes: It has no owner: no single class is responsible for it, which is exactly why there is no single place to change it.

participants.responsibility: Classes that each hold one fragment of the responsibility and depend on the others to complete it.
participants.notes: Produced most often by overzealous SRP application — one method per class is the same defect as no cohesion.

participants.responsibility: The developer who must edit every fragment for the next change, and who must remember the full list from memory.
participants.notes: The smell is invisible in any single diff; it is only visible across a series of related change sets.

use_cases: Adding a log line number: every logging call site must change, and missing one loses the field for that one path.
Speculative over-architecting of a CRUD app with layers, DTOs, DAOs and domain objects — adding one database table requires scaffolding changes across all four layers at once.
Adding a menu item in a desktop app: edit the string constants file, the delegate-registration table, the GUI wiring and the command handler.
Copy-pasted implementations of the same rule in several classes, where a bug fix must be applied to each copy.
A cross-cutting concern (audit logging, authorisation, metrics) implemented inline at each call site rather than once.
avoid_when: The behaviour is genuinely cross-cutting and must apply at many, unpredictable call sites — use an aspect, decorator, interceptor or middleware instead of moving it to one class.
The 'fragments' are in separately deployed units or teams, where a shared library is the only realistic home and each team must still call it explicitly.
The code is generated or maintained by a framework whose contract genuinely spans the files — a persistence engine, a serialisation format, a protocol codec.
Consolidating would mean a class that depends on every other class in the system; in that case the boundary is wrong at a higher level and the fix is architectural, not a Move Function.
You are mid-incident. Scattered edits are a symptom to schedule, not a defect to fix under pressure — the exception is a copy-paste block that is one edit instead of four.
pitfalls: Splitting by implementation layer rather than by requirement: a shared 'utils' class that everything calls is a god object, not a cure.
Consolidating into a class that has to call back into all the original classes, producing a cycle the move was supposed to remove.
Fixing the symptom with a cross-cutting framework when the real problem is that one requirement was mis-decomposed in the first place.
Assuming a commit that touches many files proves the smell: a genuine feature often does. The test is repeated simple changes touching the same files, not a single large one.

related_patterns_notes.facade: A facade is where a scattered cross-cutting concern can be gathered safely when it has a single narrow surface; shotgun surgery is the failure mode where the concern has no facade and every caller assembles it.
related_patterns_notes.interceptor: An interceptor is the general remedy when the scattered thing truly applies to every call site: move it out of the code rather than moving the code together.
related_patterns_notes.transaction-script: A transaction script is the alternative to a scattering rich domain model: one procedure per business operation, so the whole change is one procedure.
related_patterns_notes.data-transfer-object: A DTO is often a participant in the scattering rather than the cure — every field added to a contract propagates through the DTO, mapper, view model and fixture.
related_patterns_notes.query-object: Query objects exist so a query that would otherwise be assembled at several call sites has one home; a scattering of query fragments is a query-object smell.
related_patterns_notes.aggregate: A DDD Aggregate is an explicit commitment to change together in one place, which is the same principle shotgun surgery violates implicitly.
related_patterns_notes.domain-service: A domain service is the legitimate home for logic that genuinely spans entities — provided it does not become the place every unrelated fragment is dumped into.

anti_patterns: The four-file menu item: string constant, delegate table, UI wiring and handler, each of which is incomplete on its own.
The DTO-propagation chain: adding one field touches the entity, the DTO, the mapper, the view model, the template, the API spec and the test builders.
Copy-paste implementations of one rule, where the bug fix is a multi-file campaign and each forgotten copy is a live defect.
One-method classes: the over-split that makes Divergent Change and Shotgun Surgery two faces of the same mistake.
The 'we will update the legacy code as we touch it' promise, which produces a codebase where every file is one generation behind its neighbour.
Collecting into a shared utility module that now depends on — or is depended on by — everything, so the scatter became a hub.
Layer-per-change scaffolding: a change that must be written identically in every layer because the layers each own the same knowledge.
design_principles: Information expert: the knowledge about how to do one thing belongs in one place, and that place should be the class that can see everything the thing needs.
High cohesion within a unit, low coupling between units: cohesion is what a scattered change destroys; it is the axis you are restoring.
Single responsibility, applied to requirements and not to methods: one class per reason to change, not one class per method.
Once and only once / the abstraction principle: any behaviour that exists in more than one place is a promise you will have to keep in all of them.
Make illegal states unrepresentable: a change that must be made in several places is a state that several places can disagree about.
best_practices: Measure it from version control, not from intuition: audit the last twenty change sets and count files touched per commit. A healthy codebase implements a small feature in a few files; shotgun surgery shows up as the same files recurring.
Instrument it in review — a pull request that touches eight files for one menu item is the unit of evidence.
Prefer inlining first when the fragments are scattered: Inline Function/Inline Class, accept a temporarily large unit, then extract into a coherent one.

Use Fowler's specific recipes: Move Function and Move Field to gather; Combine Functions into Class when functions operate on similar data; Combine Functions into Transform when they enrich a structure; Split Phase when the shared part can produce input for a consuming phase.
Extract a parameter object when the scatter is in signatures rather than bodies — several methods receiving the same five parameters is shotgun surgery at the argument level.

If the change must be applied at every call site, that is a cross-cutting concern: an aspect, decorator, interceptor or middleware applies it once, and the review rule becomes 'no copy-paste at call sites'.
Consolidate one responsibility per commit, keeping the build green, so a reviewer sees the file count drop.
Add a CI check that fails when a small change touches an unexpected number of files — the cheapest guard against the smell returning.
sources: Martin Fowler & Kent Beck, 'Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code' (Addison-Wesley, 1999), 'Shotgun Surgery' — 'similar to divergent change but is the opposite', and the inlining-first tactic: https://www.informit.com/articles/article.aspx?p=2952392&seqNum=8
